lines: 3-day history of vomiting after feeding with progressive forceful emesis
The infant with congenital intestinal malrotation and feeding intolerance presents following emergency department evaluation earlier today.
The infant was born at term via an uncomplicated vaginal delivery and has been exclusively formula-fed.
The parents report that the vomiting has progressively worsened and is now forceful, shooting out several feet.
The infant appears hungry and eager to feed but becomes irritable shortly after.
- Father with history of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
- Maternal hypertension during pregnancy requiring labetalol therapy
- No known history of congenital gastrointestinal anomalies in siblings
Smoking: Never. Alcohol: Never. Occupation: Infant.
On examination, the infant is alert but appears dehydrated with decreased skin turgor and a sunken anterior fontanelle.
His weight is below the 3rd percentile for his age.
An olive-sized, mobile, non-tender mass is palpable in the epigastric region.
Abdominal ultrasonography is performed, revealing thickening of the pyloric muscle.

lines: Persistent projectile vomiting over the past 4 days unresponsive to formula changes

The patient is a male infant with congenital intestinal malrotation and feeding intolerance who returns with recurrent vomiting one month after prior hypertrophic pyloric stenosis and three months after intestinal malrotation with midgut volvulus.
His mother reports that he forcefully expels his feeds immediately after eating, often projecting the vomitus several feet.
The vomiting occurs shortly after consuming 1–2 ounces of formula and is not reduced by switching from a milk-based to a hydrolyzed protein formula.
She notes the vomitus is never green or yellow.
The infant has continued to produce daily pale, seedy stools but appears to be more irritable and hungry after each episode.
There is no family history of gastrointestinal disease
Smoking: Never. Alcohol: Never. Occupation: Infant.
Physical examination reveals a mildly dehydrated infant with normal abdominal findings and no palpable masses.
Laboratory results show a mild hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis.

The vomiting is described as non-bilious and occurs shortly after meals, leading to poor weight gain and visible hunger after episodes.
His prenatal and perinatal courses were unremarkable, with no known teratogenic exposures.

The infant has no dysmorphic features,
Laboratory studies reveal hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.
